Two basketball courts. That's how much wing one Airbus A380 has. 🏀

Together, the A380's wings cover 845 m². An official FIBA basketball court measures 28 × 15 m, or 420 m². So one superjumbo carries two full courts' worth of wing, with 5 m² to spare. Tip to tip, the wingspan is 79.8 m, longer than the aircraft itself.

Upper deck or lower deck: where would you sit? 👇

On Tuesday, 24 November, a single-engine Cessna 210 crashed into the water near Horn Island, Mississippi. All six people on board, four adults and two children, lost their lives.

The flight had departed New Orleans and was bound for Fort Myers, Florida. The U.S. Coast Guard and local agencies searched for hours before divers located everyone on board.

The NTSB is investigating, supported by the FAA. A preliminary report usually follows within about 30 days. The cause is not yet known, and we will not speculate.

In memory of the six people who lost their lives. Our thoughts are with their families and friends.

Sources: U.S. Coast Guard, FAA, NTSB (via ABC News, The Washington Post, AVweb).

On 1 November 2026, a Learjet 60 flying from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas went down in Greenacres, Florida. All nine people on board lost their lives.

At 12:47 p.m., at about 35,000 feet near thunderstorms, the crew reported light clear ice and moderate turbulence and asked to climb. According to the NTSB, less than 30 seconds later a radio call reported an overspeed condition and a descent, followed by a mayday. Investigators found the left elevator up to almost four miles from the main site. The cause has not been determined, and we will not speculate.

The full video, with everything investigators have confirmed so far, is on our YouTube channel.

Plot twist: the 'black box' isn't black. 🟠

Flight recorders are painted bright orange so investigators can find them after an accident. Most airliners carry two: a cockpit voice recorder and a flight data recorder. Both are built to survive an impact of 3,400 g and a fire of 1,100 °C for 30 minutes.

New York to London in 4 hours 56 minutes. Without Concorde. ✈️💨

On 9 February 2020, British Airways flight BA112, a Boeing 747-400, rode the jet stream of Storm Ciara across the Atlantic. Ground speed peaked at 825 mph (1,327 km/h) and the jumbo landed almost two hours early. Guinness World Records lists it as the fastest subsonic transatlantic commercial flight.

Ever noticed the cabin lights go dim before landing? It's not nap time. 💡

It's about safety: if there's an emergency, your eyes are already used to the dark. Exit signs and the floor path lighting stand out more, and with the window shades up, you and the crew can see what's happening outside.

Why do flight paths look curved on a map? 🌍

Because the Earth is a sphere. The shortest route between two points is an arc called a great circle, and flat maps stretch the world, especially near the poles. That's why flights between North America and Europe often head far north, towards Greenland.

Norse Atlantic has grounded every flight. ✈️⏸️

On Thursday (Nov 26), the Norwegian long-haul airline suspended all flights and said it will file for bankruptcy unless it secures short-term financing urgently. A day earlier it called its finances "critical", and its shares fell 85%.

Founded in 2021 to bring back budget flights across the Atlantic, Norse operates 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners. Talks with investors about a possible takeover are ongoing, but the company says there is no guarantee of a solution.

Booked with Norse? Please follow the airline's official updates. Our thoughts are with the passengers and staff affected.

Update: Norse Atlantic's Norwegian airline has filed for bankruptcy. ✈️

On Friday (Nov 27), the board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS filed at the Agder District Court in Norway, one day after the airline grounded every flight. All Norse flights are cancelled and ticket sales have stopped. Its UK sister airline has also cancelled all flights, while the parent company looks for a solution for the rest of the business.

Affected? Please don't go to the airport. Contact your travel agent, travel insurer or card provider about refunds and alternatives.

Our thoughts are with everyone affected, including the airline's employees.
